topic: Communicate to Lead: A Silver Blaze Investigation

rule_groups.name: Ch.1 · A Vanished Champion — Subject–Verb Agreement
rule_groups.explain: The verb must agree in number with its subject: a singular subject takes a singular verb, a plural subject takes the base (plural) form.

singular.label: Singular
singular.note: A singular subject (Inspector Gregory) takes a singular verb ending in -s.

plural.label: Plural
plural.text: The Scotland Yard detectives investigate the case together.
plural.note: A plural subject takes the base form of the verb, with no -s.

rule_groups.name: Ch.2 · The Alarm at King's Pyland — Articles
rule_groups.explain: Use 'a/an' for something mentioned for the first time; use 'the' for something specific or already identified; use no article with general, uncountable ideas.

definite.label: The (definite)
definite.text: Holmes examined the hoofprints beside the moor path.
definite.note: Use 'the' for something specific, already known to speaker and listener.

indefinite.label: A / An (indefinite)
indefinite.text: He noticed a strange knife lying in the grass.
indefinite.note: Use 'a/an' for something mentioned for the first time, one of many.

rule_groups.name: Ch.3 · Across the Moor — Prepositions
rule_groups.explain: Prepositions of place (in, on, at, near) locate people or things; prepositions of direction (towards, in the direction of) show movement.

place.label: Place
place.text: The stable stood on the edge of the lonely moor.
place.note: Use place prepositions (on, at, in, near) to locate people or things.

direction.label: Direction
direction.text: Holmes walked towards the gypsy camp to question the travellers.
direction.note: Use direction prepositions (towards, into, across) to show movement.

rule_groups.name: Ch.4 · Reconstructing the Night — Past, Present & Future Tense
rule_groups.explain: Simple past describes finished actions, simple present describes habits and general truths, and simple future (will + base verb) describes plans or predictions.

past.label: Past
past.text: Straker left the house quietly before midnight.
past.note: Simple past describes a completed action in a finished time.

present.label: Present
present.text: Holmes examines every clue with total concentration.
present.note: Simple present describes habits, facts, or a leader's ongoing method.

future.label: Future
future.text: Silver Blaze will run in tomorrow's big race.
future.note: Simple future (will + base verb) describes a planned or predicted event.

rule_groups.name: Ch.5 · Piecing Together the Evidence — Perfect Tenses
rule_groups.explain: Present perfect (has/have + past participle) links a past action to a present result. Past perfect (had + past participle) shows an action completed before another past action.

present_perfect.label: Present Perfect
present_perfect.text: Holmes has examined every footprint near the stable.
present_perfect.note: Present perfect links a past action to the present result — the evidence is now known.

past_perfect.label: Past Perfect
past_perfect.text: By the time Watson arrived, Holmes had already solved half the mystery.
past_perfect.note: Past perfect shows an action completed before another past action.

rule_groups.name: Ch.6 · Presenting the Facts — Active & Passive Voice
rule_groups.explain: Active voice puts the doer of the action first and sounds direct. Passive voice (be + past participle) puts the receiver of the action first — useful when the doer is unknown or the result matters more.

active.label: Active
active.text: Someone drugged the stable-boy's supper that night.
active.note: Active voice puts the doer of the action as the subject — direct and confident.

passive.label: Passive
passive.text: The stable-boy's supper was drugged that night.
passive.note: Passive voice puts the receiver of the action first — useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

rule_groups.name: Ch.7 · The Witnesses Speak — Reported Speech
rule_groups.explain: In reported speech, the tense of the original statement usually shifts one step back into the past, and quotation marks are removed.

direct.label: Direct Speech
direct.text: "I saw a stranger near the gate," said the stable-boy.
direct.note: Direct speech quotes the speaker's exact words, inside quotation marks.

reported.label: Reported Speech
reported.text: The stable-boy said that he had seen a stranger near the gate.
reported.note: Reported speech shifts the tense backward and removes the quotation marks.

rule_groups.name: Ch.8 · Weighing the Possibilities — Conditionals
rule_groups.explain: First conditional (if + present, will + verb) discusses real future possibilities. Second conditional (if + past, would + verb) imagines unlikely present situations. Third conditional (if + past perfect, would have + past participle) imagines an impossible past.

first.label: 1st Conditional
first.text: If the horse is stolen, the trainer will lose his position.
first.note: First conditional: real, possible future situations (if + present, will + base verb).

second.label: 2nd Conditional
second.text: If Holmes were less observant, he would miss the vital clue.
second.note: Second conditional: imagined, unlikely or hypothetical present situations (if + past, would + base verb).

third.label: 3rd Conditional
third.text: If Straker had been more careful, he would not have died.
third.note: Third conditional: an impossible past situation — imagining a different outcome that never happened.

rule_groups.name: Ch.9 · Giving Direction — Modals & Question Tags
rule_groups.explain: Modals like 'must' show obligation and 'might' show possibility, while question tags check understanding or invite agreement — all essential tools for a leader who communicates with clarity.

obligation.label: Obligation
obligation.text: Every officer must report new evidence at once.
obligation.note: Use 'must' or 'have to' for strong obligation — essential for clear leadership instructions.

possibility.label: Possibility
possibility.text: The missing horse might be hiding at a neighbouring stable.
possibility.note: Use 'might' or 'could' to express possibility, not certainty.

question_tag.label: Question Tag
question_tag.text: You noticed the dog's silence that night, didn't you?
question_tag.note: A question tag checks understanding or invites agreement — a useful leadership tool.

rule_groups.name: Ch.10 · The Race and the Truth — Pronouns & Punctuation
rule_groups.explain: Possessive pronouns (his, her, its, their) show ownership without repeating a noun. A semicolon can join two closely related complete sentences, and a comma often introduces a quotation.

pronoun.label: Pronoun
pronoun.text: Holmes gave his final report to Colonel Ross.
pronoun.note: Possessive pronouns (his, her, its, their) show ownership without repeating the noun.

punctuation.label: Punctuation
punctuation.text: Silver Blaze, disguised with dye, won the race; the crowd cheered wildly.
punctuation.note: A semicolon joins two closely related complete sentences without a conjunction.
